newsitem.title: GERMANY: No Blair in sight for German SPD, rivals say.
newsitem.headline: No Blair in sight for German SPD, rivals say.

text.p: German opposition Social Democrats (SPD) were inspired on Thursday by Labour's landslide British election victory but their political rivals claimed there was no SPD version of Tony Blair in sight.
"In 73 weeks we'll do exactly the same. Congratulations Tony Blair!" a billboard outside SPD headquarters proclaimed.
But Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), noting the SPD had not yet named its challenger to Kohl, promptly asked who was the "Tony Blair of the SPD".

"Of course the SPD will try to gain some inspiration from the Labour party victory, but it will also force the question 'Well, who is your Tony Blair?'," Ruprecht Polenz, a CDU member of the German-British parliamentarians' group told Reuters.
Opinion polls say Gerhard Schroeder, the media-friendly and pro-business premier of Lower Saxony state, would have the best chance of ousting Kohl, who has held power since 1982.
But the cigar-smoking maverick can only run for chancellor with the agreement of SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, who also has his sights on the top job despite losing to Kohl in 1990.
Schroeder told north German radio that Blair had shown fellow left-of-centre parties how to combine modern economic policies with social justice. "That was probably his recipe for success," he said.
Schroeder said although the SPD still had some problems to iron out, the party had long ago made many of the reforms Labour pushed through over the last few years.
Lafontaine, seen as closer to the left and his party's favourite to challenge Kohl, sent Blair a congratulatory letter.
"Your success is good for Britain and good for the whole of Europe. Let's work together to fulfil the hopes of the people of Europe for social justice and jobs with a secure future," he wrote.
The SPD said Blair had invited Lafontaine and an SPD delegation to a victory party in Britain on May 11.
Guenter Verheugen, the SPD's foreign policy coordinator, said there was no sense asking who was like Blair in Germany.
"Let's ask who the SPD in Germany can nominate and what he can learn from the methods, the style and comportment of Tony Blair," Verheugen said.
SPD party manager Franz Muentefering agreed. "We know we're not allowed to clone humans... We'll make our own decision and it will be a good one," he told West German Radio.
Muentefering said the Conservatives had been swept away after four legislative periods and vowed the SPD would do the same when Kohl's fourth term ended next year.
"Kohl will have a hard time in the next 18 months. Then, in 74 weeks we'll win the election, I'm convinced."

But Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) denied any parallels with the Conservatives. "Oskar Lafontaine is not Tony Blair and Helmut Kohl is not John Major," CDU foreign policy spokesman Karl Lamers told Hesse radio.
The CDU said Blair's victory would put the spotlight on the SPD over its chancellor candidate.
"The SPD's dilemma over its candidate will only get worse. You'll see that tomorrow at the latest, when the joy at Labour's victory has passed," said the CDU's Polenz.
CDU general secretary Peter Hintze said if the SPD would only listen to "their New Labour friends" then they would cooperate with the government on planned tax reforms.
"Tony Blair favours tax rates which the Social Democrats reject and say are from the devil," Hintze said.
